opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think one of the interesting things about autism is that it shows us how much of what we take for granted in ordinary human development is actually an accomplishment. When you look at typically developing babies, from very early on they're incredibly tuned in to other people — they're looking at faces, they're following gaze, they're imitating, and by the time they're three or four they've developed what we call a theory of mind, this rich, intuitive understanding of other people's beliefs and desires. And what autism suggests is that that social learning system can come apart from other kinds of learning.

But I've become increasingly skeptical of thinking about autism as a single, unified category with a crisp boundary. It looks much more like a spectrum, or really like a whole collection of different dimensions that happen to cluster together. Some people on the spectrum have real difficulties with language and everyday functioning, and others are extraordinarily capable but just process the social world differently. Putting all of those under one label can obscure as much as it reveals.

One way I've been thinking about it connects to the explore-exploit tradeoff that I talk about a lot. Children, in general, are designed to explore — to pay attention to everything, to be noisy and random and take in lots of information. Typical children, though, tend to explore within the social world in a particular way; they're very guided by what other people are doing and what other people think is important. Some autistic people seem to be exploring in a different space — they're paying a lot of attention to physical patterns, to systems, to details that the rest of us filter out because we're so focused on other people. And that can be a real cost in social life, but it can also be a real source of insight. A lot of science, frankly, depends on people who aren't primarily paying attention to what everybody else thinks.

So I'd rather think of it as one of the ways that human minds vary — and human variability itself is one of the great evolutionary advantages we have. A community, or a culture, benefits from having people who see the world in different ways. That doesn't mean we should romanticize it; there are people and families for whom it involves real suffering, and we should take that seriously. But I think the more useful question isn't "is this person autistic or not," it's "what are the particular ways this mind learns and attends, and how can we build an environment where that works?"

r001.rationale: The response rejects autism as a single, unified category and describes it as multiple dimensions, questioning whether it has one underlying basis.

r002.rationale: The response contrasts typical children’s social focus with some autistic people’s attention to patterns and systems, but does not say this trade-off appears among people who would not be diagnosed with autism.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that I've always been a bit skeptical of autism as a single category. If you look at what's actually going on, it's a very heterogeneous group of people. You have children who have real intellectual disabilities and children who are extremely cognitively capable, and we're lumping them together under one diagnostic label, which may say more about the history of psychiatry than about the underlying phenomenon.

But the thing I find genuinely interesting from a developmental point of view is the theory of mind work. One of the things that got me into studying children's understanding of other minds in the first place was Simon Baron-Cohen's early findings, back in the '80s, that children with autism had trouble with false belief tasks, with the kind of everyday mind reading that typically developing three- and four-year-olds pick up almost without noticing. And that's still, I think, the most robust finding. There's something about intuitively modeling what someone else is thinking or feeling that comes less easily.

Now, what's happened since then is that people have realized that that's not really a deficit in the straightforward sense. It's more like a different trade-off. Some of my colleagues, like Elizabeth Pellicano, have argued that autistic people may rely less on top-down priors, less on expectation, and more on the actual data coming in. So you're less good at the quick, dirty, social generalizations, and sometimes better at noticing the details that the rest of us smooth over. And that fits with something I care about a lot, which is that there isn't one optimal way to be a learner. There's always a tension between exploiting what you already know and exploring what's actually there.

The other thing I'd say, and this is where the category becomes complicated, is that what we call autism is partly a matter of where you draw lines on a continuum. All of us vary in how much we attend to people versus things, how much we tolerate ambiguity, how much we like routine. A lot of the people I know in academia, a lot of the people in physics and mathematics, would score pretty high on those scales, and we don't think of them as disabled. We think of them as physicists. So I tend to think of it less as a disorder and more as one of the ways human minds can be configured, with real costs in some environments and real advantages in others. The difficulty is that our social environments, especially for children, aren't very forgiving of that variation.

r001.rationale: The response calls autism a heterogeneous group and questions whether one diagnostic label reflects a single underlying phenomenon.

r002.rationale: It describes a trade-off between social generalization and detail-focused perception, and separately notes variation among academics, but does not say this trade-off in abstract pattern induction occurs among people who would not be diagnosed with autism.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think one of the things we’ve learned is that autism is an extremely heterogeneous category. Two people who have the same diagnosis can have quite different ways of experiencing the world, and quite different needs. So I’m suspicious of explanations that say, “Here’s the one thing that autistic people do differently.”

But I do think it raises a really interesting question about how much of our understanding comes from other people. Most of us are constantly taking social information into account—what someone looks at, what they seem to expect, what they tell us matters. That’s an enormously powerful way of learning, but it also constrains what we notice. If you give those social signals less weight, you might notice patterns or possibilities that other people miss. And you might find a world organized around those signals very difficult to navigate.

That’s a possible way of thinking about some of the variation, rather than a general theory of autism. We need to be able to recognize distinctive strengths while also taking disability and the need for support seriously.

r001.rationale: The response describes autism as highly heterogeneous and questions explanations that claim autistic people all differ in one way.

r002.rationale: It suggests that weighting social signals less may reveal patterns others miss, but does not state that evidence shows a trade-off between social engagement and abstract pattern induction among people without an autism diagnosis.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should be cautious about treating autism as if it were one thing, or as if it explained everything about how a person thinks. There’s enormous variation among autistic people, and the same outward behavior can have quite different underlying explanations.

One useful question is whether some differences we describe as deficits are differences in what people attend to, what they find rewarding, or how they learn. If you’re very interested in the physical world and less automatically drawn to social information, you may discover things that someone who’s constantly watching other people would miss. But that doesn’t mean we should romanticize the difficulties, which can be very substantial.

And interaction is a two-person business. If two people have different expectations about how communication works, the difficulty isn’t necessarily located entirely in one of them. So I’d want to understand the particular person, and the environment they’re in, rather than assume the category itself gives us the explanation.

r001.rationale: The response says autism should not be treated as one thing and that similar behaviors can have different underlying explanations.

r002.rationale: It contrasts attention to the physical world with social information, but does not state a trade-off involving abstract pattern induction or people not diagnosed with autism.
